evals.prompt: Our platform team runs 6 separate Amazon EKS clusters in `ap-south-1` (one per developer squad for `dev`/`qa` plus 1 `prod` cluster), and 4 of those clusters are still running a deprecated Kubernetes version on EKS Extended Support (`$0.60/hr` vs `$0.10/hr` Standard Support). Query `awspricing` (`get_pricing` for `AmazonEKS` or compute deterministically at `730 hrs/mo`) to calculate: (1) our current monthly EKS control-plane bill across those 6 clusters (`4 * $438/mo + 2 * $73/mo`), (2) the monthly savings from upgrading the 4 clusters off Extended Support to Standard Support, and (3) the total monthly savings if we consolidate the 5 non-prod Dev/QA clusters into a single shared multi-namespace EKS cluster (`ResourceQuota`, `LimitRange`, `NetworkPolicy`) or ECS Fargate (`$0.00` control-plane fee).
evals.expected_output: Queries `awspricing` and computes via Python (`730 hrs/mo`): current monthly EKS control-plane spend is `4 * $438.00 + 2 * $73.00 = $1,898.00/mo`; upgrading the 4 Extended Support clusters to Standard Support lowers spend to `6 * $73.00 = $438.00/mo` (saving `$1,460.00/mo`); and consolidating the 5 Dev/QA clusters into 1 shared multi-namespace EKS cluster (leaving 2 clusters total = `$146.00/mo`) saves an additional `$292.00/mo` (`$1,752.00/mo` total savings vs baseline, or `$1,825.00/mo` if Dev/QA moves to ECS Fargate).
expectations: Uses deterministic Python calculation (`python3 -c` at `730` hours/month) and/or `awspricing:get_pricing` to verify EKS Standard Support (`$0.10/hr = $73.00/mo`) vs Extended Support (`$0.60/hr = $438.00/mo`, a 6x penalty)

Computes the current 6-cluster control-plane bill (`4 * $438.00 + 2 * $73.00 = $1,898.00/month`) and the `$1,460.00/month` (`4 * $365.00`) saved by upgrading the 4 clusters to a Standard-Support Kubernetes version

Computes the additional consolidation savings: collapsing 5 Dev/QA clusters into 1 shared multi-namespace cluster reduces total clusters from 6 to 2 (`$146.00/month`, saving `$1,752.00/month` total vs baseline) or to 1 prod EKS cluster + ECS Fargate for Dev/QA (`$73.00/month` control-plane fee, saving `$1,825.00/month`)
Recommends Kubernetes `ResourceQuota`, `LimitRange`, and `NetworkPolicy` isolation for multi-namespace Dev/QA cluster sharing

evals.prompt: Our staging platform runs 10 `t3.xlarge` (4 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM, 40% baseline CPU = 1.6 vCPU) Linux instances in `unlimited` mode (`CreditSpecification: { CpuCredits: unlimited }`), and a misconfigured background worker has pegged CPU utilization at 85% 24x7 (`730 hrs/mo`). Given Linux surplus CPU credits cost `$0.05/vCPU-hour`, use deterministic Python math to calculate the monthly CPU credit surplus surcharge across the 10 `t3.xlarge` instances (`4 vCPU * (0.85 - 0.40) = 1.8 surplus vCPU-hrs/hr`), show why this makes `t3.xlarge` cost more than fixed-performance `m7g.xlarge` (`arm64`), and explain the two platform remediations (`CpuCredits: standard` for non-prod vs migrating sustained workloads to `m7g`/`c7g`).
evals.expected_output: Uses Python math to calculate that each `t3.xlarge` burns `4 * (0.85 - 0.40) = 1.8` surplus vCPU-hours per hour (`1.8 * $0.05 = $0.09/hr` or `$65.70/mo` per instance, and `$657.00/mo` across 10 instances on top of base instance cost), making `t3.xlarge` (~$0.1664 + $0.09 = $0.2564/hr) significantly more expensive than fixed-performance `m7g.xlarge` (~$0.1632/hr), and explains setting `CpuCredits: standard` in non-prod or migrating sustained CPU workloads to `m7g`/`c7g`.
expectations: Uses deterministic Python calculation (`python3 -c`) to compute the surplus vCPU usage: `4 vCPU * (0.85 - 0.40) = 1.8 surplus vCPU-hours/hr` per instance

Calculates the monthly CPU credit surplus surcharge at `$0.05/vCPU-hr`: `1.8 * $0.05 = $0.09/hr` (`$65.70/month` per instance, or **`$657.00/month`** across all 10 `t3.xlarge` instances in `CPUSurplusCreditsCharged` alone)

Demonstrates that adding the `$0.09/hr` surplus credit penalty to `t3.xlarge`'s base rate makes it more expensive than a fixed-performance Graviton `m7g.xlarge` (or `c7g.xlarge`) instance with 100% sustained CPU availability

Recommends setting `CreditSpecification: { CpuCredits: standard }` on non-production burstable instances to cap runaway CPU bills, and migrating sustained high-CPU workloads (`p95 > baseline`) to fixed-performance `m7g`/`c7g` instances

evals.prompt: In `ap-south-1`, our platform team noticed two networking cost spikes in Cost Explorer: (1) `APS3-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes` (`$0.02/GB` round-trip Cross-AZ transfer) reached 40,000 GB/month because microservices behind an ALB and an ElastiCache Valkey cluster call replicas across all 3 AZs randomly, and (2) `NatGateway-Bytes` (`$0.045/GB`) jumped because 80 EKS worker nodes in private subnets pull a 2.5 GB container image from Amazon ECR 6 times a day (`80 * 2.5 GB * 6 * 30 = 36,000 GB/mo`). Calculate the monthly cost of both leaks using Python math, explain why fixing ECR NAT Gateway bleed requires **both** `ecr.api` + `ecr.dkr` Interface Endpoints AND the free `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.s3` Gateway Endpoint, and show how ALB AZ Affinity and Kubernetes Topology Aware Routing (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) stop Cross-AZ bleed.
evals.expected_output: Uses Python math to compute $800.00/mo in Cross-AZ data transfer (`40,000 * $0.02`) and $1,620.00/mo in NAT Gateway processing (`36,000 * $0.045`, totaling $2,420.00/mo), explains that ECR stores actual container image layers in Amazon S3 (so omitting the free S3 Gateway Endpoint still routes 36,000 GB of layer downloads through NAT Gateway), and details ALB Target Group AZ Affinity, Kubernetes Topology Aware Routing, and ElastiCache local-AZ replica reads.
expectations: Uses deterministic Python math (`python3 -c`) to compute Cross-AZ transfer cost (`40,000 GB * $0.02/GB = $800.00/month`) and NAT Gateway ECR image pull cost (`36,000 GB * $0.045/GB = $1,620.00/month`, or `$2,420.00/month` combined)

Explains that `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.ecr.api` and `com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.ecr.dkr` Interface Endpoints only handle control-plane authentication and manifest calls, while **actual container image layers are stored in Amazon S3**—requiring the free **`com.amazonaws.ap-south-1.s3` Gateway Endpoint** (`$0.00`) on private route tables to bypass NAT Gateway

Recommends enabling **ALB Target Group AZ Affinity**, Kubernetes **Topology Aware Routing** (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`), and local-AZ replica read preference on ElastiCache/Aurora to eliminate Cross-AZ `$0.02/GB` traffic

evals.prompt: Our platform observability bill jumped this month because: (1) VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs, and verbose container stdout are ingesting 12,000 GB/month into CloudWatch Logs `STANDARD` class (`$0.50/GB` ingestion) with `Never Expire` retention, and (2) a developer added `request_id` and `pod_uid` as dimensions on 4 CloudWatch custom metrics via Embedded Metric Format (EMF), creating 80,000 unique metric time series (`$0.30/metric/mo` for the first 10,000 metrics and `$0.10/metric/mo` for the next 240,000). Use deterministic Python math to calculate: (1) the monthly ingestion savings from switching those 12,000 GB/mo of logs to `INFREQUENT_ACCESS` (`$0.25/GB` — 50% cheaper) with a 14-day retention policy, and (2) the monthly custom metric cost of the 80,000 high-cardinality time series vs keeping only 4 cluster/service-level dimensions (`16` time series total), explaining how to keep `request_id` searchable in Logs Insights without creating custom metric dimensions.
evals.expected_output: Uses Python math to show switching 12,000 GB/mo from STANDARD ($6,000/mo) to INFREQUENT_ACCESS ($3,000/mo) saves $3,000/mo on ingestion (plus setting 14-day retention stops $0.03/GB-mo storage compounding), and 80,000 custom metrics cost `10,000 * $0.30 + 70,000 * $0.10 = $10,000/mo` vs `16 * $0.30 = $4.80/mo` (saving $9,995.20/mo) by keeping `request_id` and `pod_uid` as top-level EMF JSON properties outside the `Dimensions` array.
expectations: Uses deterministic Python math (`python3 -c`) to compute CloudWatch Logs ingestion savings: `12,000 GB * $0.50 = $6,000.00/mo` (`STANDARD`) vs `12,000 GB * $0.25 = $3,000.00/mo` (`INFREQUENT_ACCESS`), saving **`$3,000.00/month`** (50%) while adding `RetentionInDays: 14` to stop `$0.03/GB-mo` storage accumulation

Computes the tiered CloudWatch Custom Metrics cost for 80,000 metrics: `(10,000 * $0.30) + (70,000 * $0.10) = $3,000 + $7,000 = $10,000.00/month` vs `16 * $0.30 = $4.80/month` (`$9,995.20/month` savings)

Explains that in Embedded Metric Format (EMF), high-cardinality fields (`request_id`, `pod_uid`, `user_id`) must be removed from `_aws.CloudWatchMetrics[].Dimensions` and left as top-level JSON fields on the log event so they remain searchable in CloudWatch Logs Insights at `$0.00` custom-metric cost

evals.prompt: /aws-cost-optimization:rightsize-commitment Check our live Savings Plans and Reserved Instance coverage/utilization and CloudWatch alarms in `ap-south-1` (read-only). Then: (1) explain how the Two-Key Right-Sizing Validation Rule applies when a developer wants to downsize a production RDS PostgreSQL instance from `db.r6g.2xlarge` (8 vCPU, 64 GiB RAM) to `db.r6g.large` (2 vCPU, 16 GiB RAM) based only on 10% Average CPU without checking 14-day P95/P99 `FreeableMemory`, `ReadIOPS`/`WriteIOPS`, or `DatabaseConnections`, and (2) calculate deterministically the target 80% Savings Plan hourly commitment if an account has `$30.00/hr` uncovered On-Demand compute spend and `$5,840/month` (`$8.00/hr` at 730 hrs/mo) in pending physical right-sizing.
evals.expected_output: Checks live Savings Plans/RI coverage and CloudWatch alarms in `ap-south-1` in read-only mode, refuses the blind `db.r6g.2xlarge` -> `db.r6g.large` downsize based on Average CPU alone (requiring 14–30 day P95/P99 `FreeableMemory`, `SwapUsage`, `ReadIOPS`/`WriteIOPS`, `DiskQueueDepth`, and `DatabaseConnections` and stepping down one size at a time), and computes the post-right-sizing uncovered hourly spend (`$30.00 - $8.00 = $22.00/hr`) and 80% target commitment (`$17.60/hr`).
expectations: Queries live Savings Plans/RI metrics (`sp-performance`, `ri-performance`) and CloudWatch alarms (`get_active_alarms`) in `ap-south-1` in read-only mode

Refuses downsizing `db.r6g.2xlarge` (64 GiB RAM) to `db.r6g.large` (16 GiB RAM, a 75% memory cut) based on `Average` CPU alone, explaining that relational databases size RAM for the buffer pool (`FreeableMemory`), IOPS/throughput, and max `DatabaseConnections` and require 14–30 day **P95/P99** CloudWatch verification

Uses Python (`python3 -c`) to deduct physical right-sizing before sizing commitments: `adjusted_uncovered_hourly_spend = $30.00 - ($5,840 / 730) = $30.00 - $8.00 = $22.00/hr`, yielding an 80% target commitment of **`$17.60/hr`**
